sweep_summary: Pulaar (pula1263) is coded 'weight' from Niang 1995 (KWPL 20), and nothing found in this sweep moves that. Five target items: (1) Wiltshire 2006 (open Cascadilla PDF, on file and read) restates Niang 1997 exactly as the catalog has it (heaviest non-final syllable CVVC>CVV>CVC>CV, leftmost on ties, initial default, final never stressed except monosyllables) — confirms. (2) Niang 1995 is the catalog's own deciding source (Glottolog 'already_listed=false' is a bibliography gap); copied into the audit dir and re-read — confirms. (3) Prunet 1989 (CAAL 6, De Gruyter DOI 10.1515/9783110884890-010, paywalled): the Google Books opening snippet shows it is an analysis of the voice/aspect system via length 'redistribution', and a search-within of the volume for 'stress' has no hit in pp. 138-160 — prosody-but-not-word-stress, silent, low priority. (4) Anyanwu & Diallo (FAB 17: 65-89, Köppe, paywalled): a Google Books snippet reads 'In Fula, it is primary stress that is more relevant. Generally, the first syllable of the word receives the stress, irrespective of length' — potentially in tension with weight-sensitivity, but the paper (title: 'word accent mobility') was not read and the variety is probably Guinean Pular (Diallo's specialty), so relevance to pula1263 is unclear; high priority to acquire. (5) Zubko 1973 (Russian, Olderogge Festschrift p. 396ff; title supplied from a Google Books TOC snippet, Glottolog has it 'wanting'): print only, content unread, medium priority. Extra find: McLaughlin & Wiltshire 2017 'Syllable weight in the phonology of Pulaar' (Benjamins, DOI 10.1075/cilt.338.10lau, paywalled; snippets restate the Niang/Wiltshire generalisations for Mauritanian/Fuutankoore Pulaar) — worth adding to the bibliography. searches ran to automated fetch (Crossref, Glottolog, Google Books feed, Köppe, kunstkamera); DDG/Bing/Mojeek/Brave/HathiTrust/S2/OpenAlex were blocked or rate-limited. new_statements.reading: Weight-sensitive, unbounded-from-the-left primary stress on the heaviest non-final syllable (CVVC > CVV > CVC > CV), leftmost on ties, initial default, final syllable never stressed except in monosyllables; secondary stress on remaining heavy syllables unless clash. This is the same system the catalog codes from Niang 1995 (weight, default initial), now with the monosyllable exception and secondary-stress rule stated explicitly. It is a restatement of Niang 1997, not independent fieldwork, so it corroborates rather than replaces the deciding source.
new_statements.check: confirmed by a second reader, with minor differences

audit.reasoning: Quote check: the deciding passage, the domain passage and the conclusion passage are all verbatim in the held ERIC PDF of Niang 1995 at the stated pages (56, 61, 67). Deciding source: a 1995 native-speaker working paper wholly on Pulaar word stress, superseded in form (not content) by the author's 1997 UPA monograph. Best-available check: Glottolog 5.1's 137 descriptive refs for pula1263 contain no reference grammar with a stress chapter that outranks Niang; the dedicated stress literature is Niang 1995/1997, Wiltshire 2006 and Mc Laughlin & Wiltshire 2017 (Diop 1998 UIUC dissertation, restricted, covers syllable/vowel processes but lists no stress chapter in its abstract). I fetched sources the open Wiltshire 2006 (Cascadilla) to; its statement of primary stress (pp. 181-182) and secondary stress (pp. 186-187), based on Niang 1997 plus informan

sources.quote: Generalizations The last syllable of the word is never stressed. Stress the first syllable if there is no heavy syllable in the word as in (7). [...] Stress the penult syllable if it is the only heavy syllable in the word as in (8). [...] When both first and penult syllables have the same structure CVC, CVV or CVVC, stress the first syllable as in (9). [...] When both first and penult syllables are heavy but with different weight, stress the heaviest syllable. CVVC is heavier than CVV which in turn is heavier than CVC which is heavier than CV as in (10).
sources.note: This is the catalog's deciding source, re-read: final syllable extrametrical, heaviest non-final syllable wins on a four-way scale, leftmost on ties, initial default. p. 53 also summarises earlier Fula accounts (Taylor 1953: stress depends on long vowels; Arnott 1970: first syllable salient; McIntosh 1984: last non-final CVC/CVV else initial; Prunet & Tellier 1984: first heavy syllable from the left, else initial). Glottolog's 'already_listed=false' is a bibliography bookkeeping gap: the work is our deciding source.
